compliance.notes: Re-scored on BCP's complete 2026/27 pack after the capital and budget documents were supplied by hand; the earlier assessment_caveat is CLEARED (explicit "") because the capital-strategy content is now in evidence and the residual gaps are BCP's, not ours. BCP publishes no standalone capital strategy: its capital strategy is a section of the Cabinet budget report of 11 February 2026 (paras 66-82, 'The capital strategy is based on the following core principles'), with the Capital Investment Programme (Appendices 7 and 7a) and the 2026-2031 Strategic Asset Management Plan (Appendix 8) as its substance, all recommended to full Council (recommendations viii-x, unchanged by the 10 February addendum). STRONGEST: the liability benchmark (separate General Fund and HRA charts plotting all four balances to 2095); the capital expenditure / financing / CFR chain (five-year GF and HRA tables in the TMS, reconciled to a four-year programme by directorate and by scheme); the borrowing strategy and its candid handling of the projected over-borrowed position driven by cash-flowing the DSG/SEND deficit; the MRP policy (annuity asset-life, £12.8m of VRP overpayments disclosed); the creditworthiness policy (ratings plus a CDS overlay); and the S151 officer's s25 affordability and reserves advice. WEAKEST, and now confirmed as real gaps rather than missing documents: no financing-costs-to-net-revenue-stream ratio for either fund (PI-07), no upper/lower limits on the maturity structure of borrowing (PI-09) and no fixed/variable interest-rate exposure limits (RISK-02) — three core indicators absent from a 'Treasury Indicators' section that sets only the operational boundary and the authorised limit (and those as a single combined line, in a table headed £'000 whose figures are £m). On the commercial side the supplied capital documents confirm that BCP holds non-treasury investments (investment properties within a £2.16bn estate, council-owned companies and joint ventures, a £15.3m development exposure at Carters Quay) but nowhere quantifies them: no proportionality test against reserves (COM-03, core), no schedule of non-treasury investments by purpose (COM-04), no net commercial/service income ratio (PI-08) and no income-dependence or contingency disclosure (COM-07). Also absent: the promised specified/non-specified investment sections (INV-05), a portfolio risk-exposure indicator (INV-06), any derivatives policy (RISK-06) and any flag on audit qualification of the source data (RPT-05). The Treasury Management Policy, Practices and Schedules document (TMS para 82, 'will be presented alongside') is not in the pack, which limits TMP-01 and GOV-02 but nothing core.

gaps.evidence: TMS p.16 para 80 'The maximum period for investments will be 5 years'; p.15 para 75 sets time limits by counterparty type (local authorities 5 years, Banks 1 higher quality 2 years, Banks 1 medium quality 1 year, DMADF 6 months).
TMS p.10 para 59 reproduces the substance of Prudential Code para 51 and Budget report p.20 para 67 commits every borrowing-funded business case to the PWLB borrowing restrictions.

TMS p.24 Appendix 3: the S151 officer is responsible for 'ensuring the proportionality of all investments so that the Authority does not undertake a level of investing which exposes the Authority to an excessive level of risk compared to its financial resources'; TMS p.6 para 32 asks members, by approving the CFR figures, to 'consider the scale proportionate to the Council's remaining activity'; Budget report p.37 acknowledges exposure to council-owned companies and joint ventures.

news_drafts.headline: BCP Council reports £179.8m schools deficit, with grant to cover 90% awaiting government approval of its plan
news_drafts.lead:
Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole Council has built up a deficit of £179.8m on its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) as at 31 March 2026, according to the corporate risk register put to its Audit and Governance Committee on 15 October. Most of it arises from high needs funding, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities.

In 2025/26 the council budgeted £64.5m for high needs, but spending approached double that. The gap was financed through temporary borrowing of £57.5m. The government has announced a high needs stability grant intended to cover 90% of the accumulated deficit, but payment depends on the Department for Education approving the council's local plan for reforming special educational needs provision. The council submitted its plan by the 19 June 2026 deadline and expected a decision in September. The register says approval "remains outstanding", so the grant is not confirmed. A statutory override, a temporary government rule that keeps the deficit off the council's main balance sheet, expires on 31 March 2028.

The council has received £2,487,876 of first-year reform funding to set up its "Experts at Hand" model and start delivery from September 2026. The register says the council's red spend controls, imposed to manage overspends in the current year, have paused the recruitment needed. It adds that this places the council at risk of the Department for Education reclaiming the money.

news_drafts.headline: BCP Council's schools-funding deficit forecast at £275.5m by March 2027, with SEND plan awaiting approval
news_drafts.lead:
Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole Council expects the deficit on its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) to reach £275.5m by March 2027, up from £179.8m, according to its first-quarter budget monitoring (the in-year check of spending against budget). The in-year shortfall is projected at £95.7m. The cause is support for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), known as high needs: the high-needs budget is £68.4m and spending is more than double that. The council calls this its biggest financial risk.

Its main mitigation depends on government approval of a SEND reform plan, submitted in June, with the outcome still awaited. If approved, a High Needs Stability Grant would cover 90% of the deficit as at 31 March 2026, roughly £162m of about £180m, with payment due in autumn 2026. Further support is expected for the 2026/27 and 2027/28 deficits.

The council is also investing. In March 2026 it committed £13.9m of capital spending (money spent on things that last) on specialist and alternative provision over three years, plus £300,000 for accessibility work, alongside a £9.2m allocation from the Department for Education. The 2026/27 reform programme has £2.47m, 80% of it for staffing. The council reports 319 additional specialist places delivered and 224 in development, though its own assessment says provision is still short of demand. A new board is overseeing a plan to recover the in-year deficit.

news_drafts.headline: BCP Council forecasts £275.5m schools deficit by March 2027; government grant covering 90% awaits approval
news_drafts.lead:
Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole Council expects the accumulated deficit on its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) to reach £275.5m by March 2027, up from £179.8m at the start of the year. The first-quarter budget monitoring report (the in-year check of spending against budget) puts the deficit for 2026/27 alone at £95.7m. It is driven by the cost of placements for children with special educational needs and disabilities, which the council identifies as its most significant financial risk.

A new high needs stability grant, announced in the 2026/27 local government settlement, is intended to cover 90% of the deficit as it stood on 31 March 2026. It depends on government approving the council's local SEND reform plan, which was submitted in June; the outcome is awaited. If approved, the grant would be paid in autumn 2026. Government has also said it expects to offer similar support for further deficits in 2026/27 and 2027/28, though not without limit, and that from 2028/29 SEND funding is expected to rise to fully fund expected spending.

The reform plan also carries capital spending (money spent on things that last) of £13.5m for 2026/27, made up of £8.9m of high needs grant and £4.6m of Special and Alternative Provision grant. The capital investment report says £4.1m of the high needs grant is "yet to be allocated to specific projects", and the Special and Alternative Provision money is not yet committed to approved schemes. Spending in the first quarter was £163,940. The council expects works to proceed through the summer and autumn holidays.

findings.paper_title: Annual Report of Internal Audit Counter Fraud Work and Whistleblowing Referrals 2025/26
findings.headline: Three formal whistleblowing referrals received and investigated during 2025/26, all concluded in accordance with policy
findings.detail: The council received and investigated three formal whistleblowing referrals during the financial year 2025/26 (1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026). All cases were concluded in accordance with the Council's Whistleblowing Policy. Full details are contained in confidential appendices.
findings.matters: Whistleblowing framework completion and reporting demonstrates that governance structures for staff to raise concerns safely are operating and documented; this is a component of audit committee assurance on internal controls and staff confidence in reporting mechanisms.
findings.quote: Three formal whistleblowing referrals were received and investigated during the 2025/26 financial year (1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026). Details are included in Confidential Appendix A. All cases were concluded in accordance with Council's Whistleblowing Policy.

findings.paper_title: Annual Report of Internal Audit Counter Fraud Work and Whistleblowing Referrals 2025/26
findings.headline: 946 Blue Badges and concessionary travel passes cancelled through NFI matching against deceased person records
findings.detail: National Fraud Initiative data-matching against national deceased records identified and led to cancellation of 164 Blue Badges and 782 concessionary travel passes that were being held by individuals recorded as deceased. This represents automated prevention of ongoing unauthorised access to benefits and services following individuals' deaths.
findings.matters: Large-scale cancellation of benefits following death demonstrates material control effectiveness and prevention of ongoing fraud loss; this is an ongoing audit control that recurs annually and prevents a flow of losses.
findings.figures: Blue Badges cancelled: 164; Concessionary travel passes cancelled: 782; Total: 946
findings.quote: 164 Blue Badges were cancelled as a result of matches against deceased national records. 782 concessionary travel passes were cancelled as a result of matches against deceased national records.

findings.paper_title: Annual Report of Internal Audit Counter Fraud Work and Whistleblowing Referrals 2025/26
findings.headline: Housing tenancy fraud referrals increased 30% to 48 in 2025/26, attributed to improved working arrangements and fraud awareness
findings.detail: Housing tenancy fraud referrals rose from 37 in 2024/25 to 48 in 2025/26. The council reports this may reflect closer working arrangements with Housing Officers and increased fraud awareness among officers within the Housing Allocations Team. No properties have been recovered from these referrals in either year.
findings.matters: Increasing housing tenancy fraud detection indicates either rising fraud risk or improved detection; the council attributes this to better awareness and inter-team working, suggesting detection is the driver rather than worsening fraud environment.
findings.quote: Housing Tenancy referrals increased during 2025/26, which may reflect closer working arrangements with Housing Officers and increased fraud awareness among officers within the Housing Allocations Team.

findings.paper_title: Annual Report of Internal Audit Counter Fraud Work and Whistleblowing Referrals 2025/26
findings.headline: Counter fraud investigation and prosecution spending increased to £121,749 in 2025/26, up 3% year-on-year
findings.detail: The council spent £121,749 on investigation and prosecution of fraud in 2025/26 (aggregate salaries and on-costs), compared to £118,134 in 2024/25 and £97,548 in 2023/24. This reflects the council's increased resource allocation to counter fraud activity as part of its commitment to zero-tolerance approach to fraud and corruption.
findings.matters: Growing counter fraud spend is justified if fraud is being detected (as it is); however, ongoing investment in a fraud team that is recovering c.£67k from NFI work and detecting hundreds of cases is a legitimate control cost that a finance director needs to monitor and justify against recoveries and prevented losses.
findings.quote: Total amount spent by the authority on the investigation and prosecution of fraud. (aggregate salaries + on-costs) £121,749 £118,134 £97,548

findings.paper_title: Annual Report of Internal Audit Counter Fraud Work and Whistleblowing Referrals 2025/26
findings.headline: CIPFA counter fraud best practice assessment achieved 94% score with conclusion council is meeting fraud and corruption risk management standard
findings.detail: An independent annual assessment using CIPFA's fraud risk management tool achieved a score of 94%. CIPFA concluded that the council is meeting the standard set out in its Code of Practice on Managing the Risk of Fraud and Corruption, with robust arrangements in place, a counter fraud strategy backed by resources, and proactive and effective response. CIPFA noted that whilst no organisation is fraud-proof, the council has taken robust steps to ensure its resilience.
findings.matters: Independent validation of the council's counter fraud control environment provides assurance to lenders and audit committee that governance and risk management frameworks are mature; this supports credit rating and borrowing assessments which rely on audit quality and control effectiveness.
findings.quote: The organisation is meeting the standard set out in the CIPFA Code of Practice on Managing the Risk of Fraud and Corruption. The leadership has acknowledged its responsibilities for managing the risks and it has robust arrangements in place to identify and manage risks.
